name: Luvale
catalog_quote: Each word in Luvale has one main stress, which is an important factor in word division. The stress of words in Bantu is typically on the penultimate syllable. (Horton 1949:18) [...] In most words, stress is mostly on the penult of the root. In monosyllabic roots, stress tends to fall on penultimate prefixes, or a suffix is attached. In some morphologically determined cases stress is antepenult or…

audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (penultimate, dom=true, strict=false), domain WORD with a note that verbs take stem-penult and that morphologically determined antepenult/final and prefix-stressed monosyllabic-stem forms exist (Horton 1949:10-14 via SPA 1979; StressTyp2 passage 1312 and its 'Exceptional (Luvale)' + 'Compound_very irregular_' pattern rows). Confirm against Horton pp. 10-14 when borrowed.
audit.deciding_source_kind: database or survey citing another work
audit.reasoning: Quote check: the two second-hand passages the record relies on are verbatim in held files (SPA 1979 djvu text p.065; StressTyp2 SQL passages 1311-1312, words 1448-1453), but the primary, Horton 1949, is not held (archive.org borrow-only; inside-search API refused), so 'partly-confirmed'. Deciding source: a 1979 database digest and a 2015 database summary of a 1949 missionary reference grammar; no later stress description of Luvale was found (Crossref 'Luvale'/'Lwena' return only Kawasha 2008 syntax and ethnography; TUFS holds Yukawa 1986/1987 tonal studies, both already held and silent on stress; Hyman 2009 fetched sources, silent; Kashoki & Mann 1978 held elsewhere, generic and does not name Luvale). Horton 1949 is therefore probably still the best source and we do not hold it. Coding risk: even the held digests contradict 'strict' -- SPA: 'Stress tends to be penultimate... some exceptions amon

sources.quote: None for Luvale; general claim that 'penultimate' prominence in E/S Bantu usually means phrase-penultimate lengthening, and that some Bantu languages 'are said to lack stress altogether'.

sources.quote: 'There is no long vowel in this language.' ... the falling tone mark 'usually appears only on the penultimate syllable ... The vowel with [falling mark] on it is phonetically falling in the sentence-final position.' No statement about stress in the introduction; the paper is a tonal analysis.
